Q20202007.summary: Within a deeply undercut border of acanthus leaves, two scenes are stacked one above the other. Above, the haloed Christ, followed by apostles, hands or receives a cloth with an apostle beside a tall tiled building; below, Christ stands among the apostles while a man bends before him, taking his hands with a covered cloth before another small building. Crisp and lively in its carving, the plaque shows the vivid narrative style of later Carolingian ivories.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to about 850–900, records it as French and notes traces of paint on the ivory; it measures about 9.9 × 7.8 cm.
It was acquired for The Cloisters Collection in 2000 (accession 2000.486).
Q20202007.notes: Wikidata classed this as a painting dated 850; it is a carved ivory plaque. The precise subjects of the two scenes were not confirmed, so no scripture is given.

cur:catacombs-mp-baptism.summary: A naked young figure stands frontally in the water while, above him, the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from the top left. The scene is the Baptism of Christ, painted in the shorthand of the catacombs: the Baptist is reduced to a hand and part of a figure at the upper edge, and everything centres on the Son on whom the Spirit rests.
facts: The descending dove distinguishes the Baptism of Christ from ordinary baptism scenes in catacomb painting.
The Catacomb of Marcellinus and Peter on the Via Labicana covers about three hectares with 4.5 km of galleries on three levels.
cur:catacombs-mp-baptism.notes: Commons gives no date or provenance details for this file; the date given here is approximate.

cur:objects-magdeburg-ivory-incredulity-.summary: Beneath a tiled roof the apostles stand behind a low wall in three arches; in the left-hand arch the haloed, risen Christ raises his right arm while Thomas bends forward to touch the wound in his side. In the centre a firmly bolted door recalls that Christ came to the disciples 'when the doors were shut'. The architectural setting turns the Gospel episode into a vivid image of the risen Lord present among his Church.
facts: It is one of the 16 surviving Magdeburg Ivories commissioned by Otto I, each measuring nearly 13 by 12 cm (Wikipedia).

rijks:BK-2025-29.summary: This small cast figure, once fixed to a cross, shows the dead Christ with his head sunk forward, his arms stretched almost horizontally and his legs slightly bent and parallel beneath a knotted loincloth. Traces of gilding still cling to the metal. Such corpora were made in numbers for altar and processional crosses in the Romanesque period, bringing the image of Christ's sacrifice close to worshippers.
facts: The Rijksmuseum dates the figure between 1000 and 1130 and attributes it to an anonymous German workshop.
It stands only 12 cm high and was given to the museum in 2025 by Jan van Adrichem and Martijn van Nieuwenhuyzen.
rijks:BK-2025-29.notes: The date range runs into the 12th century; y set to the midpoint. The third sentence of the summary is general context, not a museum statement.
